source_text: Odisse debemus istos conuentus et coetus ethnicorum, uel quod illic nomen dei blasphematur, illic in nos quotidiani leones expostulantur, inde persecutiones decernuntur, inde temptationes emittuntur. quid facies in illo suffragiorum impiorum aestuario reprehensus? non quasi aliquid illic pati possis ab hominibus (nemo te cognoscit Christianum), sed recogita, quid de te fiat in caelo. dubitas illo enim momento, quo diabolus in ecclesiam furit, omnes angelos prospicere de caelo et singulos denotare, quis blasphemiam dixerit, quis audierit, quis linguam, quis aures diabolo aduersus deum ministrauerit? non ergo fugies sedilia hostium Christi, illam cathedram pestilentiarum ipsumque aerem qui desuper incubat scelestis uocibus conspurcatum? sint dulcia licebit et grata et simplicia, etiam honesta quaedam. nemo uenenum temperat felle et elleboro, sed conditis pulmentis et bene saporatis, et plurimum dulcibus id mali inicit. ita et diabolus letale quod conficit rebus dei gratissimis et acceptissimis imbuit. omnia illic seu fortia seu honesta seu sonora seu canora seu subtilia perinde habe ac stillicidia mellis de lucunculo uenenato nec tanti gulam facias uoluptatis quanti periculum per suauitatem.
thought_title: Flee the gatherings where God is blasphemed
orientation: Tertullian is addressing Christians directly, urging them to hate and avoid the public gatherings of pagans because there God is blasphemed and the devil works against the church.
pass_a_gloss: We ought to hate these gatherings and assemblies of pagans, either because there the name of God is blasphemed, there daily lions are demanded against us, from there persecutions are decreed, from there temptations are sent out. What will you do, having been blamed in that meeting-place of impious votes? Not as if you could suffer anything there from men (no one knows you as a Christian), but think again what is done about you in heaven. Do you doubt that at that very moment, when the devil rages in the church, all the angels look forth from heaven and mark each one, who has spoken blasphemy, who has heard it, who has supplied his tongue, who his ears to the devil against God? Will you not therefore flee the seats of the enemies of Christ, that chair of pestilences and the very air which from above is befouled with wicked voices? Let them be sweet, it will be allowed, and pleasing and simple, even some honorable things. No one mixes poison with gall and hellebore, but with seasoned dishes and well-flavored ones, and mostly with sweet things he throws in that evil. So also the devil steeps the deadly thing which he prepares with the things most pleasing and most acceptable to God. All things there, whether strong or honorable or sonorous or melodious or subtle, regard just as drops of honey from a poisoned little vessel, and do not value the gullet of pleasure as much as the danger through sweetness.

choices.why: Both nouns denote public gatherings; 'conuentus' is a coming together, 'coetus' an assembly; 'ethnicorum' is rendered 'pagans' per glossary.
rejected: conventions and gatherings of the heathen

choices.why: The word literally means a tidal inlet or boiling place, but here it is used metaphorically for a turbulent assembly place of votes; 'meeting-place' preserves the spatial sense without over-interpreting.
This echoes Psalm 1:1's 'seat of pestilence' language; 'chair' keeps the literal cathedra and the plural genitive 'pestilences' is retained.

choices.english: drops of honey from a poisoned little vessel
choices.why: The image is of honey dripping from a small poisoned container; 'drops' for stillicidia, 'little vessel' for the diminutive lucunculus, 'poisoned' for uenenato.
rejected: drippings of honey from a poisoned jar

choices.why: Gula is literally the throat or gullet; the phrase means the appetite for pleasure, and 'gullet' preserves the bodily metaphor.

bible_refs.note: cathedram pestilentiarum echoes the 'seat of pestilence' of Psalm 1:1, which Tertullian quoted earlier in section 3.

pass_b_english: We ought to hate these gatherings and assemblies of pagans, if only because there the name of God is blasphemed, there the daily lions are demanded against us, from there persecutions are decreed, from there temptations are sent out. What will you do when you are singled out in that meeting-place of unholy votes? Not that you can suffer anything there from men, for no one knows you are a Christian, but consider what is happening to you in heaven. Do you doubt that at the very moment the devil rages against the church, all the angels look down from heaven and mark each person: who has spoken a blasphemy, who has listened, who has lent his tongue, who has lent his ears to the devil against God? Therefore you will not flee the seats of Christ's enemies, that chair of pestilences, and the very air above, befouled by wicked voices?

Let the shows be sweet, pleasing, and simple, even honorable in some respects. No one serves poison by itself, with gall and hellebore; he puts the evil into seasoned dishes, well flavored and mostly sweet. So too the devil steeps the deadly thing he makes in the things most pleasing and acceptable to God. Treat everything there, whether brave, honorable, loud, melodious, or subtle, as drops of honey from a poisoned little vessel, and do not make the gullet of pleasure worth as much as the danger that comes through sweetness.

problems.source_quote: non ergo fugies sedilia hostium Christi, illam cathedram pestilentiarum ...
problems.why: The Latin passage has no Psalm citation; Psalm 1:1 does not mention pestilences.
problems.fix: that chair of pestilences, and the very air above, befouled by wicked voices

problems.quote: Will you not then flee the seats of Christ's enemies
problems.source_quote: non ergo fugies sedilia hostium Christi
problems.why: Latin states a negative assertion (you will not flee); English turns it into a question, altering the claim.
problems.fix: Therefore you will not flee the seats of Christ's enemies
problems.ruling: Latin 'non ergo fugies' is a negative statement: 'you will not flee.' English makes it a question 'Will you not flee,' changing the assertion.

edits.old: that chair of pestilences (Psalm 1:1), and the very air above, befouled by wicked voices?
edits.new: that chair of pestilences, and the very air above, befouled by wicked voices?

edits.old: Will you not then flee the seats of Christ's enemies
edits.new: Therefore you will not flee the seats of Christ's enemies

fixed: Removed the erroneous Psalm 1:1 citation; the Latin has no scriptural reference here.
Changed the rhetorical question to a negative assertion to match the Latin 'non ergo fugies'.

problems.quote: No one mixes poison with gall and hellebore; he puts the evil into seasoned dishes
problems.why: Gall and hellebore ARE poisons; sentence contradicts itself—means no one serves pure poison, but disguises it in tasty food.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'No one serves pure poison; he mixes the evil into seasoned dishes'.

edits.old: No one mixes poison with gall and hellebore; he puts the evil into seasoned dishes
edits.new: No one serves poison with gall and hellebore; he puts the evil into seasoned dishes

fixed: The source says 'nemo uenenum temperat felle et elleboro' — no one mixes poison with gall and hellebore, i.e., no one serves poison alongside bitter substances; the point is that poison is disguised in sweet food. The English 'mixes poison with gall and hellebore' is ambiguous but not wrong; however, 'serves' clarifies the intended sense without changing the meaning.

last_rejected.quote: Let the shows be sweet, pleasing, and simple, even honorable in some respects.
last_rejected.source_quote: sint dulcia licebit et grata et simplicia, etiam honesta quaedam.
last_rejected.why: Latin 'dulcia' means sweets/food, not 'shows'; misidentifies subject and violates glossary.
last_rejected.fix: Let the sweets be pleasant, simple, and even somewhat honorable.
last_rejected.ruling: 'sint' is subjunctive 'let them be'; context is shows/spectacles. 'dulcia' can describe shows as sweet/pleasing, not only food.

polish.changed: Clarified the poison metaphor so it no longer contradicts itself, smoothed sentence rhythm, and made the implied subject of the final exhortation explicit.
